source_refs.note: Exercise 14.1, Question 2: book page 266 (PDF 271); answer key PDF 311 (book page 306).

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Find the magnitude of the vector \(\underline{v}\) and write the direction cosines of \(\underline{v}\): \(\underline{v} = 3\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Two things are asked: the length of \(\underline{v}\) and its direction cosines.
The direction cosines are \(\cos\alpha = x/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\beta = y/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\gamma = z/|\underline{v}|\).
Plan: find \(|\underline{v}|\), divide each component by it, then check the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{v} = 3\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 6\underline{k}\), so \(x = 3\), \(y = -2\), \(z = 6\).
To find: \(|\underline{v}|\) and \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\); the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector \(\underline{v}/|\underline{v}|\).

Find the magnitude
\[|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-2)^2 + 6^2}\]
\[= \sqrt{9 + 4 + 36}\]
\[= \sqrt{49} = 7\]
Why: Pythagoras in three dimensions; squares of negative components are positive.

Divide each component by \(|\underline{v}| = 7\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{3}{7}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{-2}{7}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{6}{7}\]
Why: In the right triangle formed with each axis, cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse = component / length.

Check
\[\dfrac{9}{49} + \dfrac{4}{49} + \dfrac{36}{49}\]
\[= \dfrac{49}{49} = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: For every vector \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\) (the Important Result of 14.1.8).

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Find the magnitude of the vector \(\underline{v}\) and write the direction cosines of \(\underline{v}\): \(\underline{v} = -4\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Two things are asked: the length of \(\underline{v}\) and its direction cosines.
The direction cosines are \(\cos\alpha = x/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\beta = y/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\gamma = z/|\underline{v}|\).
Plan: find \(|\underline{v}|\), divide each component by it, then check the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{v} = -4\underline{i} + 4\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\), so \(x = -4\), \(y = 4\), \(z = 2\).
To find: \(|\underline{v}|\) and \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\); the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector \(\underline{v}/|\underline{v}|\).

Find the magnitude
\[|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{(-4)^2 + 4^2 + 2^2}\]
\[= \sqrt{16 + 16 + 4}\]
\[= \sqrt{36} = 6\]
Why: Pythagoras in three dimensions; squares of negative components are positive.

Divide each component by \(|\underline{v}| = 6\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{-4}{6} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\]
Why: In the right triangle formed with each axis, cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse = component / length. Fractions are reduced.

Check
\[\dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{1}{9}\]
\[= \dfrac{9}{9} = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: For every vector \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\) (the Important Result of 14.1.8).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Find the magnitude of the vector \(\underline{v}\) and write the direction cosines of \(\underline{v}\): \(\underline{v} = -6\underline{i} + 8\underline{j}\).
blocks.explanation:
Two things are asked: the length of \(\underline{v}\) and its direction cosines.
The direction cosines are \(\cos\alpha = x/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\beta = y/|\underline{v}|\), \(\cos\gamma = z/|\underline{v}|\).
Plan: find \(|\underline{v}|\), divide each component by it, then check the squares add to 1.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{v} = -6\underline{i} + 8\underline{j}\), so \(x = -6\), \(y = 8\), \(z = 0\).
To find: \(|\underline{v}|\) and \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\).
Method: \(|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\); the direction cosines are the components of the unit vector \(\underline{v}/|\underline{v}|\).

Find the magnitude
\[|\underline{v}| = \sqrt{(-6)^2 + 8^2 + 0^2}\]
\[= \sqrt{36 + 64 + 0}\]
\[= \sqrt{100} = 10\]
Why: Pythagoras in three dimensions; squares of negative components are positive.

Divide each component by \(|\underline{v}| = 10\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{-6}{10} = -\dfrac{3}{5}\]
\[\cos\beta = \dfrac{8}{10} = \dfrac{4}{5}\]
\[\cos\gamma = \dfrac{0}{10} = 0\]
Why: In the right triangle formed with each axis, cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse = component / length. There is no \(\underline{k}\) term, so \(z = 0\) and \(\cos\gamma = 0\) (\(\gamma = 90^{\circ}\)).

Check
\[\dfrac{9}{25} + \dfrac{16}{25} + 0\]
\[= \dfrac{25}{25} = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: For every vector \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\) (the Important Result of 14.1.8).
